[VS_00s] || Oṃ, homage to Śiva. ||

Having prostrated before the god Bhāskara, the bestower of the boons of worldly enjoyment and liberation, I shall proclaim the teaching for the ascetics for the sake of the welfare of all the world. (1)

[VS_01j] Lord Śivāditya is the one to whom I bow; he is the deity of all. May he bestow grace for both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). Worldly enjoyment is prosperity (*abhyudaya*); liberation is the supreme good (*kaniḥśreyasa*). What is the purpose of my bowing to him? "I shall proclaim the teaching on the observances (*vratiśāsana*).
I, the master, shall cause the teaching to be maintained by the ascetics (*saṅ viku*).
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, and for the happiness of the world; it is as follows:
When a wise person indeed guards both the restraints (*yama*) and the observances (*niyama*), by that very guarding of them, his intellect is not shaken. (2)

[VS_02j] O wise one, listen! The *yamavrata* and the *niyamavrata* are the guardians of the self; for if one guards the *yamavrata* and *niyamavrata*, one’s intellect does not waver. Such is the *yamavrata*.
Non-violence, celibacy, truthfulness that is not deceptive, and non-stealing—these five are the restraints (yamas) proclaimed by Rudra. (3)
Non-violence is that which does not cause distress.
Brahmacarya is the state of being free from sexual union with women, as well as the practice of reciting mantras related to the life of a celibate student.
Truly, you are one who speaks the truth.
That which is not subject to conventional usage is not conventionally expressed.
Non-stealing is the absence of any deficiency regarding the property of others. This is the fourth; it is called the *yama-vrata*. Thus spoke Lord Rudra.
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food, and vigilance—these five are proclaimed as the observances (niyamas). 4.
[VS_04j§1] What is the nature of non-anger? It is the absence of malice toward others.

Service to the guru is the root that causes the perfection of one's own duties toward the guru; such is the nature of devotion to the guru. It serves as the cause for the guru to bestow his various secret instructions.
Purity, constant bathing, sipping water, and attendance upon the sun.
Worship of the Lord.
Lightness of food means not eating excessively at every meal; this is heedfulness.
The state of being diligent is the practice of the venerable Lord of Men. This is the fifth observance (*niyamavrata*), as stated by the Lord Śiva:

"This is the observance of restraint and discipline (*yama-niyamavrata*) which the ascetic (*viku*) must protect at all times, because his mastery of the sacred observances depends upon it; for if he does not guard it, his intellect will inevitably become fickle. That is precisely why one should avoid speaking with those who are wicked, ending even with the mention of forbidden food (*abhakṣya*)."
Drinking what should not be drunk, and approaching those who should not be approached; these are the various forms of misconduct.

[VS_04j§3] Furthermore, that which is the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsāvrata*) is the cause of the cessation of anger, delusion, pride, arrogance, and envy. The cause of these is desire; it is of various kinds, some of which are mutually contradictory. Moreover, there may be a person who commits violence for the sake of the Dharma. There is no fault in such a case. As for that person who commits violence for the sake of the Dharma—toward all sentient beings—when it is done for the purpose of performing *caru* offerings to the gods, offerings to the ancestors (*pitṛpūjā*), hospitality to guests (*atithipūjā*), or ritual offerings (*balikarmapūjā*), there is no fault in him if it is so. Nevertheless, this must be done with careful discrimination regarding what is to be killed.
(Emendation: *hiṃsan* or *hiniṅsa*) | What are these?
The swan, the horse, the *ṅūniyūni* bird, the peacock, and the buffalo. He does not kill them; he is a non-violent person (*ahiṃsaka*), and thus he is worthy of honor.

What kind of sacrificial animal (*burvan*) is this that is to be killed? It may be any wild animal, bird, or fish, such as a monkey, a squirrel, or the like. There is no fault for a practitioner (*viku*) who kills in such a manner, provided it is done for the purpose of sacrifice. Furthermore, those that are suitable to be killed [are as follows].

Every living being is devoid of *dharma* and devoid of *yoga*; that which constitutes their movement is a transformation of the body. As for its manifestations, they include such things as jumping, leaping, and so forth. All these various forms of behavior, whether in their seeking, their eating, or their drinking, may be considered [as such]. Furthermore, there are those who cause harm to the causes of bodily transformation. That which is devoid of *dharma* is a sign; it is appropriate for the practitioner (*viku*) to eliminate it. Whether in the house of one’s own teacher, in the house of one’s disciple, in the house of one’s father or mother, or in the house of one’s friends, or even in the house of one’s preceptor (*guru*), or in the house of the preceptor’s son—there is no fault for the practitioner in harming [the harmful] in such places. If there is a predator on the path—a snake, a scorpion, a rat, or a wild beast—that enters into one’s presence, there is no fault for the practitioner in harming it, because his purpose in doing so is self-protection. Furthermore, there are those who are wicked in every way and are difficult to subdue.
Thus says the Balinese manuscript (and the Devanagari *kasikəpa*):

"That [person] is worthy to be served by a monk who has attained mastery (*amatyana*), because he possesses no fear, having already transcended it. It is fitting for a monk to cause harm to one who has already transcended and who has been instructed; indeed, that person is one who, being new, must still be guided according to his capacity."
[VS_04j§5] He indeed was compassionate toward his parents, toward his wife, and toward his children;
yet he was also compassionate toward his own self.
His intellect was not clouded by evil, and he was always devoted to his religious duties. He never caused harm to living beings.
(Hiṃsaka, Apriya, Avaka)

If he is a killer, it is appropriate for him to be so; however, if he kills those who have committed offenses against him, that is a sign [of his virtue]. It is not a fault if he is a killer. Furthermore, if he has a wife of immoral character and daughters who are wicked, and he does not discipline them—that which causes his wife to behave badly—it is not his fault if he does not discipline them. If he were to discipline them, it would be appropriate for him to be so; yet, if one considers the nature of such a situation, it is because they are stubborn.
(Ed.:
*kasrəg agəna*) His head was not yet fully formed; his hair was still sparse. There is no fault in it being thus.

[VS_04j§6] As for one who kills a snake for the sake of food, he is indeed guilty of that act; such is the case with a monk (*viku*). However, if his intention is not to cause harm, then he is not at fault. He is merely practicing the use of sound and hand, and he is practicing the use of the sword; he is merely acting out of fear. There is no fault in him if it is so, because such a person is called a "protector from fear. This is the meaning of the answer.
(What is its name?
|| Its form is one; it is supported by that which is being struck (em.
[ms ka] hiniṅsakən).

If he is unskilled, his consecration (saṃskāra) is not appropriate. That ascetic must be protected from the cause of transgression, ending with the act of killing; for that cause is the absolute absence of the propriety of vocal sound, which is extremely fickle. Moreover, he is unskilled in non-violence (ahiṃsā). It is fitting that he be so, for there is no expiation (prāyaścitta) for one who is unfit [for such a role]. This is precisely why the ascetic must never fail to exert effort in guarding the vow of non-violence.
Who is this person who practices the holy life?

Regarding one who dwells with a woman: its manifestations here are as follows: the white celibate (*śuklabrahmacārī*), the black celibate (*kṛṣṇabrahmacārī*), and the variegated celibate (*śabalabrahmacārī*). The white celibate is one who does not consort with women at all; he keeps his organ tucked away. The black celibate is one who dwells with women, though he remains under the supervision of his teacher; he acts with a motive for the sake of turning them away [from misconduct].
(Emendation:

*vyāvartitena*) | He has abandoned service to his gurus; he has become arrogant toward the noble beings (*saṅ hyaṅ kabhujaṅgan*); furthermore, he has turned away from the determination of the noble science of power (*saṅ hyaṅ balavidyā*).
He excelled in logic, grammar, astrology, and the ritual worship of the sacred scriptures according to the tradition of the learned;
furthermore,
he was skilled in the duties of a householder.
Having killed him,
his head was severed; then his head fell again and again.
The master of my vow is he; I am a Kṛṣṇabrahmacārī.

[VS_04j§8] What is a variegated religious student (*śabalabrahmacārī*)? It is one who, while serving his teacher, nevertheless dwells among householders; he harbors many desires, yet his primary aim is the increase of his offspring. He performs worship at the time of sexual union, according to the proper season and place, and maintains a household.
That head belongs to a suitable wife.

The lineage of his sons shall be free from disease; indeed, he shall have many wives, yet he shall remain without sons. If that woman of his is virtuous, then at every stage of her pregnancy—both at the time of conception and at the time of sexual union—he shall not be excited during the act of intercourse. This is the cause of his lack of virility regarding the objects of sensual pleasure, for if he were to become excited...
(Emendation: *akiṃcanaśaktiḥ*, though the manuscript reads *ka kiṃnaśaktaḥ*)

Woman gives rise to the fault of desire (*kāma*). From desire arises anger; from anger arises greed; from greed arises delusion (*moha*); from delusion arises intoxication (*mada*); from intoxication arises envy (*mātsarya*); from envy arises the tendency to violence. This is why one must avoid the objects of the senses, especially the object of woman. There is no end to the conduct resulting from attachment to women, such as approaching those who should not be approached. Such is the corruption of the intellect; it leads to the ruin of even a monk through such acts—committing adultery, violating the wives of teachers, and so forth.
Sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached means having intercourse with women other than one's own wife.

The mother, daughter, granddaughter, daughter-in-law, and sister—these are the women who must not be approached for sexual intercourse (*agamyāgamana*). To take another man’s wife as one’s own wife—that is the conduct of a monk;
it is not blameworthy.

One falls into the world of hell; such is the power of Yama. It is the same regarding approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*); the sin is heavy, and one is cast into the depths of the pit, where one is punished by Yama. Whatever exists within that pit is its very essence—the gnashing of teeth, the tearing of flesh, the snapping of jaws, the crushing, and the rending. Everything within that pit is indeed its essence. Furthermore, the sin of approaching the teacher’s wife (*gurvaṅganāgamana*)—taking as one's own wife the woman who is the teacher’s consort, or repeatedly violating the teacher—is grave. Such a person is forbidden (*pantən*). However, if it is a monk (*viku*) who approaches one who should not be approached, he is called "fallen" (*patita*); he is included among those who are forbidden. That is the reason why... [the text continues].
The wise man strives to protect his celibacy (*brahmacarya*). This is the second: the sacred vow of Yama.
[VS_04j§9] What is truth?

Truth is when a practitioner (*viku*) is truthful in speech; he exerts effort in what he utters, and his mind is not untruthful, for words are many in their capacity to deceive. Furthermore, one must avoid harsh speech (*vākpāruṣya*); whatever one speaks, let it be only that which is meaningful, and one should not utter idle chatter.
Do not speak words that provoke anger;
otherwise, you will surely be cursed by your own oath.
"Pisuh pisuh! This is my word; this is my oath and my curse. Furthermore, he must be truthful in his conduct and in his observance of vows, for a monk who is not truthful in his vows is unworthy."

[VS_04j§10] Regarding the conduct of one who has attained the vow of the Siddhānta: as for what is required of one who has attained the vow of the Siddhānta, it is fitting that he should be so; however, there is this reason why he does not eat here.
Humans, monkeys, cows, tigers, elephants, horses, dogs, donkeys, chickens, pigs, and lions—all these are unclean meat. 5cd–5ab.

[VS_05j] The flesh of a dog, the flesh of a crow, the flesh of a cow, the flesh of a horse, the flesh of a monkey, the flesh of a goat, the flesh of a human, the flesh of a donkey, the flesh of a house-dweller, the flesh of a village-dweller, and the flesh of a lion—all these are termed *acokṣamāṃsa* (impure meat).
The crocodile, the water-monster, the cat, and likewise the mouse;
the mongoose, the frog, the serpent, and all unclean meat. 6.

[VS_06j] Furthermore, the following are impure meats: meat from the stomach, meat from the rectum, meat from the anus, meat from the heart, meat from the liver, meat from the gallbladder, meat from the kidneys, meat from the lungs, meat from the spleen, meat from the mesentery, meat from the intestines, meat from the colon, meat from the bladder, and meat from the urethra—all these are called impure meats.
The flesh of earthworms, maggots, and insects is despised by the whole world;
and all the various forms of living beings are merely the flesh of the lowest.
Furthermore,
this living being is a worm; I am a ground-worm.

Regarding the parts of the upper body, such as the head: the *bhūkīṭa* (earth-insects) are ants and moths within the house; likewise, all kinds of living beings that are eaten and consumed by all people—those various living beings with diverse forms, such as spiders, crickets, locusts, *irisirispoh*, *kavdivdi* ants, scorpions, and so forth—are not to be disregarded. All of these together are designated as *kaniṣṭhamāṃsa* (the lowest flesh). As for those designated as *camah* (large), they are the wild animals (*mṛga*). According to the doctrine of the one of pure vows (*śuddhabrata*), [these are forbidden].
The components of the *luvak* [are]:
the *viṅsaṅ* and the *laṅkapa*.

Onion, garlic, leeks, mushrooms, fungi, raw meat, blood, excrement, urine, human flesh, dog meat, elephant meat, horse meat, monkey meat, snake meat, lizard meat, fish, and scorpions: these are not fit to be eaten by one who follows the Siddhānta and maintains pure vows.
Crows, owls, vultures, hawks, herons, cuckoos, and female weavers;
parrots, śukas, and sārikas—all these eat unclean meat. 8.
[VS_08j§1] The limbs of the cruel-winged bird: *gagak*, *dok*, this *bakikuk* (ed.:

*ayaṁ bakikuk*), *uluṅ*, *trilaklak*, *kak*, *tuvutuvu*, *domdoman*, *atat*, *syuṅ*, *nori*, *cod*, *gagandyan*, *alapalap*, *bibido*, *daryas*; these are the "knowing birds. It is not appropriate for them to be food for that Siddhāntin.
(Siddhāntavrata:
The blue-winged bird is always [forbidden]. As for this bird, it is called *naraśabda*, *koci*, *caṅkiluṅ*, *dədəkcu*, *tikustikusan*, *jalak*, *salviriṅ jalak*, *tetek*, and *sulindit*.
It must not be eaten.
That is the ascetic.

Furthermore, among five-nailed creatures (*pañcanakha*), these are fit for consumption: the boar (*varāha*), the hedgehog (*laṇḍaka*), the porcupine (*vayava*), the tortoise (*kūrma*), and the pangolin (*bulus*). Among pangolins, there are two kinds: the *pəñu* and the *pəñu-baniṅ*. Furthermore, those fit for consumption are the wild boar (*celeṅ alas*), the forest fowl (*ayaṃ vana*), the buffalo (*mahiṣa*), the *vaḍus*, the *bañak*, the *itik*, and the *dara*. Furthermore, those fit for consumption are the *tiṅgiliṅ*, the *kidaṅ*, the *mañjaṅan*, and the *kañcil*. As for birds, they are fit for consumption when they have been summoned by a call.
Furthermore:
the deer, the *aḍava*, the *hijowan*, the *vuruvuru*, the *purukutut*, the *traguku*, and the *putər*. Moreover, these birds are fit to be eaten. (Alternatively:
"Moreover, this bird is fit to be eaten.")

The *valiviś*, *bayoṅ*, and *kalvaṅ*—these are what may be eaten. The *ivak lvah* and the *sāgara* fish are also fit to be eaten. However, one must not include the *vuhaya*, nor the *mīna* that is extremely deep in its belly; for its form is exceedingly cruel. Furthermore, those [other types] are fit to be eaten by one who follows the *Siddhānta* of pure vows (*śuddhabrata*).
[This is] the *siddhāntavrata*;
this is what is offered here.
The meat of the kaləbvan,
the lalər, the namuk, the tiṅgitiṅgi, the məriṅməriṅ, the tuma, and the kapiñjal.
(Thus Bal., kapiñjala Dev.),
*catakcatak*, *limpit*, *təṅu* | If it is mixed in this way, it is not suitable for consumption.

Furthermore, that is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*): do not eat the head, drink the blood, or consume the entrails; for those who desire great wealth, they will be very abundant. This is the essence (*kahara*).

Furthermore, that which has been touched by a snake is likewise [polluted] when touched by this [person]; moreover, if it has been touched by a dog, it is defiled. Furthermore, one must not consume anything that is subject to doubt. Moreover, one must be pure; do not eat what is impure. For example, if one eats what has been touched by a *śūdra*, all those people who are considered to be born as *caṇḍālas* will become afflicted with leprosy (*kohutakna*).
How could such a thing be?

Furthermore, it is improper for one who is exhorted by the teachings of the *vrata* to act in such a manner; it is not fitting for a noble person (*bhujaṅga*) to do so. A monk (*viku*) must not consume what is unfit to be consumed (*abhakṣya-bhakṣaṇa*), nor drink what is unfit to be drunk (*apeya-peya*). "Unfit to be drunk" refers to that which is not suitable for drinking, such as the bark of the *varagaṅ*, the *badhyaṅ*, the *savalan*, and the *budur*. These are not drunk by those who follow the *Siddhānta* and maintain pure vows (*śuddhavratas*).
What is that which he drinks?

It is not appropriate for one who observes the *siddhānta* vows to drink *brəm*, *kilaṅ*, *madhu*, *tampo*, *brəm cina*, or *yeka vnaṅ*. Likewise, even if it is a mixture (*campur*) in its vessel, once it has been tasted by another person, it is also not appropriate for him to drink it, because that mixture has become defiled. However, if there is a practitioner of the *siddhānta* vows who drinks what is not appropriate for him to drink, he is ignorant of the cause if he does not know when it was mixed; if he knows at the end [of the meal], he must perform a penance (*prāyaścitta*). He should offer the penance to his own guru. But if the penance is too heavy, it is permissible for him to act in such a way. Furthermore, if it was done with the motive of delusion (*moha*), [the rule is different].
Pride and intoxication arise from one’s own greatness; they do not arise from another. This is the point: it is not permissible to disparage others.

Regarding this, the venerable ascetic said: "The conversation between us has been very brief. This is because the venerable ascetic has made an effort to protect the sacred teaching of the Siddhānta. He has attained the vow of truth (satyavrata) and shall ascend to the supreme state (paramapada) when the proper sequence is completed. This is the third sacred vow, the vow of self-restraint (yamavrata)."
The gateway of Śikhājihva-Śiva is guarded by women, sons,
and Śūdra children.
One must not eat the flesh of a corpse, nor should there be contact with a corpse. 9.

Furthermore, there is this Siddhānta of the well-restrained and pure-vowed: the topknot (*śikhā*) and the tongue, as well as the gate of Śiva (*śivadvāra*). One must never associate with those who are impure, such as those of mixed caste through union with women, or those of the *śūdra* class, including the *caṇḍāla* and others—even those born as *caṇḍālas*. For all of these are specifically marked as distinct from the Siddhānta of the pure-vowed.

[VS_09j§2] Furthermore, one must not eat the head of a dead person, nor the cooked rice mixed with the body of a dead person, nor the various impurities associated with the corpse. One should not associate with a dead person. Moreover, it is improper for a practitioner of the Siddhānta to consume the remains of a corpse as food, nor to wear clothing that has been in contact with a corpse or its impurities, nor to wear anything that has touched a dead person. It is not right for him to handle all of these; such is the rule.
[VS_09j§3] Furthermore, there is another: "Let the scripture be the authority;

do not give it the status of worldly convention (*pavyavahāra*). It is not that he is without convention; rather, its purpose is such that it serves as a protector of the substance (*dṛvya*). For instance, consider the case of land: the substance is the earth itself. However, such is the reason for this.

(Emendation: *makataṅguhaniṅ ed*) "He who has accomplished [his purpose] and possesses truth; he who is a monk (*viku*) free from worldly affairs (*mavyavahāra*); let him not associate with the wicked. For if he is excessively attached, when the occasion arises for others to bring about a dispute regarding his property—[a dispute] that is like a thicket of tangled vines—the property that was once hidden will become manifest and be lost to him by others. This is the reason why it is better for him to be free from worldly affairs."
Furthermore, it is the protection of his wife, his son, and all his possessions;

the protection of the *poma-homa* (the fire sacrifice), as well as the protection of the teacher’s property, the protection of the teacher’s wife and family, and the protection of his sons and daughters. He is one who does not engage in worldly disputes.

[VS_09j§5] Now, when one has attained the state of a *siddha*, his own karma becomes auspicious; he is fit for non-transaction (*amavyavahāra*). Non-transaction belongs to the ascetic (*viku*) by virtue of his detachment and his lack of worldly involvement; he does not engage in activity, because the ascetic is free from the cycle of rebirth (*madolavəlya*).

He who lends money at interest (*pihutaṅ*) and buys and sells on credit (*madol avli ulahnira*), his effort is in vain. He will not receive any further profit, such as silver or compound interest (*cakravṛddhi*). He is unskilled in the methods of buying and selling, as well as in lending and borrowing; he is dead to the business of trade and has no concern for debtors or creditors, for he is entirely unfit to lend money. This is the reason for his constant distress: "Do not lend money! Do not buy and sell on credit with a monk! Even if he repeatedly begs, entreats, implores, supplicates, or flatters, all his actions are not virtuous; it is only fitting that he should be so.

[VS_09j§6] Indeed, when one has killed a human being, a monkey, a cat, a dog, a *vḍus*, a *bañak*, an *itik*, or a goat—this is the destruction of the body (*vnaṅvnaṅ*) that he undergoes at the time of day. Yet he undergoes further refinement (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) once more; thus, indeed, is his very nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, if it does not happen, it is fitting; for that state of being a beast (*kabhujaṅgan*) has vanished.

[VS_09j§7] What should be given by that monk? Whatever he has received as alms from person to person, there is no fault in his eating it all at once. [Number: 1. A handful (*muṣṭigraha*) is a *sagəgəm* [measure]. Its measure is: all its parts together, according to what is available.
[Number: 1. *Kalvi* (em. [ms. gha]; *kalviṅ* in the edition) is 5.
Thus, the *santul* [is calculated]. Whatever he eats, let it not be too much. If he is ill...
Even if he lives in a house that is not his own place, yet eats and sleeps with the owner, there is no fault of theft in him if it is done in such a manner.

Furthermore, it is said that one who possesses the limbs [of virtue], who is not deceitful, and whose theft is thus [described] is fit to be sought out by those who possess the same qualities; this refers to one who is equal in nature. Let there be no ascetic who is deceitful, if he lacks both [virtue and wealth], as well as the object of theft which is equal in nature, if it lacks both [value and ownership]; the sin committed by him becomes manifest. However, if his seeking is performed [righteously], his sin shall vanish.

Furthermore, even if a person has died and is lying in a grave, they may still have many remaining desires. It is appropriate for one to give to such a person who possesses wealth; indeed, one should be content and not be foolish. It is evident that one does not avoid sin; therefore, one must guard the vow of non-stealing (*asteyavrata*). This is the fifth among the noble *yamavrata* vows. || 0 ||

What indeed is that which is called anger? It is a calamity for this very moment, for there is no enemy like anger. There is a verse concerning this, the meaning of which is as follows: There is no friend equal to knowledge, and no enemy equal to anger;
There is no affection equal to that for one's offspring, and no power greater than fate. (10)
[VS_10j§1] Who?
[There is no friend equal to knowledge. There is no friend who cuts through suffering like knowledge; it is the most excellent of all friends.
O venerable Śāstra,
please attend to the heart of Your Majesty.
That is easy to understand; it is explained through reasoning and practice.
There is no enemy equal to anger; there is no enemy like anger. One’s own enemy does not perish until it is struck down; whereas anger, when it is provoked by another, perishes along with that other.

It is hidden within the heart. Whatever task is undertaken, it will not be accomplished unless one who knows its secret essence applies himself to it. What is the reason for this? The venerable Śrī Luṅhā says: "His youthfulness has vanished."
There is no affection equal to that for one's offspring;
there is nothing more difficult than a child.
There is no power superior to fate; when one's strength fails, it is fate that remains.

The divine ordinance has been transgressed; the meaning of the words of the verse is thus: "One who speaks with anger is indeed censured. This refers to a practitioner (*viku*) who does not abandon the state of anger; the cause for this is that he fails to attain the vow of non-anger (*akrodhabrata*), which is the first among the sacred vows of restraint (*niyamavrata*).
What is service to the teacher?

Thus it was said: "The *sārisāri* (the antelope) does not bite the feet of its teacher; it does so for a specific purpose, out of reverence for the teaching of the ascetic (*viku*), so that it may not fall into a wrong path. For if the antelope were to show such reverence toward the ascetic from its teacher, it would not find pleasure in discerning what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected (*heyopādeya*) regarding the five precepts (*pañcaśikṣā*) and the ten virtues (*daśaśīla*). This is also stated in the *Kriyopadeśa* scripture: [it teaches] the path for attaining both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). That is precisely why the conduct of the ascetic consists of service to the teacher; this is the second divine rule (*niyamavrata*)."

[VS_10j§3] What is purity (*śauca*)? It is constant purity and worship. As for the manner of that purity and worship: it is to have faith in Lord Śivāditya; to perform the service of the Sun (*sūryasevana*); to perform the practice of Śiva (*śivānuṣṭhāna*); to apply sacred ash (*bhasma*); and to recite mantras (*japa*). It is fortunate if one masters the rules for bathing (*snānavidhi*). Such is purity. This is his third observance of restraint (*niyamavrata*).

[VS_10j§4] Lightness of food, contentment with whatever is eaten, and the endurance of hunger—this is because the ascetic (viku) who seeks the delicious flavors of food merely to satisfy his own palate will find that his mind becomes agitated. It is certain that he will eventually fall into the habit of choosing and eating what is unfit for consumption. For this reason, lightness of food is indeed a virtue; it is the fourth divine vow of restraint (niyamavrata).
Heedfulness (apramāda)

The manner of diligent practice: one must be attentive toward one’s guru and follow his conduct. Its forms are as follows: *śivārcana* (worship of Śiva), *adhyāya* (study), *adhyāpaka* (teaching), *svādhyāya* (recitation), *vrata* (vow), *dhyāna* (meditation), and *yoga* (union). *Śivārcana* is one who knows the illumination of the *praṇava* within the worship of the Lord (*bhaṭāra*). *Adhyāya* is one who studies all the scriptures (*sarvaśāstra*). *Adhyāpaka* is one who instructs his disciples in the study of all the scriptures. *Svādhyāya* is one who recites the essence of what he has studied from the teacher. *Vrata* is one who is firm in his vows, such as fasting and so forth. *Dhyāna* is one who contemplates the Lord, the subtle deity who is the object of worship. *Yoga* is the meditative absorption of the vital breath (*prāṇasamādhi*), and furthermore, it is one who understands the sacred teaching (*upadeśa*) regarding the path for attaining liberation through the practice of this purpose. This is why it is practiced by the ascetic (*viku*).

[VS_10j§6] A mendicant should avoid these things: sleeping during the day, bathing, wearing ornaments, using perfumes, playing musical instruments, singing, reciting, dancing, and watching performances. He must have no doubt regarding any of the scriptures and must be absolutely diligent in the practice of the Dharma. Furthermore, he should not stay overnight in the house of anyone who is a slave, a servant, a prostitute, a eunuch, or a slave-girl; nor in a house where no one lives, or where there is no opportunity for alms. Even if there are many people living there, the mendicant should not stay overnight. This is the rule for when it is cold or hot. However, if there is a bed and a mattress provided, and it is known that the place is suitable for alms-gathering and there is no danger to the life of the host, there is no fault in staying there—even if it is cold and hot. But if there is a bed together with a mattress, it is appropriate to stay there. In any case, even if there are many people, the mendicant should not stay overnight in a place where there is much foot traffic. As for traveling: if he travels among the *caṇḍāla* caste, he may stay there as long as it takes to pass through; even if it is cold or hot, he must not consider himself superior to them. Thus says the scripture: here are its verses: *Śloka:* The wise man, having abandoned all worldly attachments, Should dwell in solitude, practicing the Dharma with diligence. He should not stay in the houses of those who are impure, Nor in places where there is no opportunity for alms. Even if there are many people, he should not stay overnight; For the sake of his own discipline, he should remain vigilant. If he travels among the low-born, he should endure the conditions there; He must not look down upon them, for they are his equals in suffering. Thus it is taught in the sacred texts. *Śloka:* The mendicant who has cast off all bonds, Should wander alone, free from attachment. In cold or heat, he remains steadfast, Never neglecting the path of truth. Even if he stays among the outcaste, He does not become their equal in pride. This is the teaching of the masters. *Śloka:* One should not stay in a place of much noise or distraction, Nor where there is no purity of heart. Whether in a village or a forest, The wise man remains focused on his goal. Thus ends the instruction.
The liquor-distiller, the worm-eater, the incendiary, the potter, and the metal-smelter—these five are proclaimed to be Caṇḍālas. ||11||

Furthermore, there are the five types of *caṇḍālas*, such as the washerman (*lavan*) and others. These five are: the man who carries corpses, the man who deals in impure things, the butcher, the hunter, and the man who smelts gold. These are the five types of *caṇḍālas* whose places of residence are unfit for one to frequent, such as their dwellings. A spiritual practitioner (*viku*) should not associate with such people, for they exceed the eighteen types of *caṇḍālas*. Furthermore, their speech is not to be listened to; even if they speak politely, it is only for the sake of milking them, which results in provocation. Therefore, a spiritual practitioner must be attentive regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; this is my vigilance. This is the fifth, the sacred rule of *niyama-vrata*.

[VS_11j§2] Indeed, one who has mastered the essence of the venerable *yama*, *niyama*, and *vrata*; who possesses the constant practice of *śīla* (virtue), *yukti* (method), and *maryādā* (discipline); who is eternally devoted to the feet of the Guru; who has received the instructions; whose conduct is never deficient; who is capable of investigating the venerable *Kalpas* (scriptures); who is well-versed in the excellent *varavaraka* of the venerable *Guru* and *Upādhyāya*; who knows how to practice the *svādhyāya* (recitation) under the *Upādhyāya*; who is capable of teaching and so forth; who does not neglect the service of the Sun; who performs worship to the Lord (*Bhaṭāra*); and who is attached to the ritual acts, such as the venerable *Śivānuṣṭhāna*, the sequence of worship (*pūjākrama*), the worship of the *liṅga*, the *pañcabalikarma*, the rules for *homa*, the procedures for the deceased (*śavavidhāna*), the *tilamūrti*, and the rules for initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*); who is learned in the supreme instruction (*paramopadeśa*) of the venerable ones; and who is that which is entrusted by the Lord of Yogins (*Yogīśvara*)—such a person is fit to dispel the impurities of others, and especially those of his own kin. He is worthy to be a Guru, provided he has been initiated and has remained [in office] for ten years.

[VS_11j§3] One must indeed avoid those who are deficient in the qualities of a most excellent teacher (*varavara-guru*). If one’s characteristics are contrary to what is expected, how could he be suitable for initiation? Even if he has reached an advanced age, he is not fit to receive the grace of the divine rite of initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*), because the ascetic (*viku*) must exert effort in performing the divine rite of initiation; otherwise, it would be as unpleasant as the taste of bitter gall.

[VS_11j§4] Indeed, it is not fitting for one who does not know the venerable *dīkṣā* ritual, nor the venerable *antyādhvan*, nor that which is discarded by the supreme Lord of Yogins (*paramayogīśvara*), to perform initiation. For he would be without initiation; and even if he were to receive special honors and be praised by others, such a person merely acquires the opposite of excellence and is praised by others. A monk must not be like this, for he will instead incur the reverse consequence and commit a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), since his mind has departed from the conduct of justice (*nyāyavṛtti*).

Who is worthy to be given initiation? One who knows the sacred *dīkṣā* procedure; one whose impurities have been purified by the sacred *Antyādhvā*; and one who has mastered the sacred *upadeśa*. He must constantly practice the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs; he must be highly capable in worship, recitation (*japa*), fire sacrifice (*homa*), yoga, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). He must not be weary of serving the sun; he must be devoted to the performance of his duties. He must know the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and vows (*vrata*). He must be patient toward his disciples; he must not be fickle. If he were to pamper his disciples, they would surely transgress the boundaries of proper conduct due to his indulgence.
