From indulgence arise many faults; from striking arise many virtues.
Therefore, a wise person administers correction to their sons and students. (12)

[VS_12j] Why? Because there is no fault in the nourishing of the intellect. This nourishing arises from the free will of one's own mind. However, if it has the striking as its cause, then by necessity many qualities arise therein; that is why even the cow-elephant (*gavaya*) is tormented [by it].

"O son and disciple! Behold that wise man! Do not envy the virtues of my son and disciple; do not be envious, for such envy is a cause for me to become angry and resentful. Because of this, it will cause confusion in the intellect of my son and disciple. Therefore, he spoke thus: 'Such a person is clearly manifest as one who is subject to rebirth.'"
For instance, some children, being untrained,
having strayed onto wrong paths due to their father’s negligence or excessive affection, are shunned by all people.
They bring about fault and great ill-repute. ||13||
[VS_13j] What? It is the rarity: that those disciples have not been trained; therefore, train them thoroughly and repeatedly.
Due to his father's negligence;
because of his father's condition;
or out of excessive affection.
Alternatively, O Rāma, if there were an excess of causes for the extreme destruction of one’s father, then what?
If it were otherwise, they would be "those who go upon a wrong path. This is certainly so, for [such people] transgress the principles of moral boundaries (*maryādā-yukti*).
They are shunned by all people;
whatever they think, it causes distress to everyone. Because of their immoral conduct, they bring great infamy upon their father.

Furthermore, there is the evil reputation of the father; why is it that he has such faults? The cause of these faults is indeed wickedness; his nature is very stubborn when he tries to correct his son. That is why people call such a father "one who steals his own offspring. Moreover, there is another statement from the scripture:
Nevertheless, some disciples have been thoroughly trained,
either through their father’s exertion or out of great affection;
they are virtuous and praised by the multitude of all people.
By their virtues, they indeed lead their father’s great fame to its full extent.
[VS_14j§1] Who? Even though they have not been marked in that way, if they have been well-trained in the rare [teachings], they are those who have trained themselves;
they are not fools.
The father [acts] with effort;
the effort caused by the mother is for the sake of the son. Or rather, the effort caused by the mother is for the sake of the father. If it is so, then they are well-behaved (*suśīlinaḥ*).
How is it that they possess such excellent virtue?
They are praised by the multitudes of all people;
they are lauded by the assemblies of all beings.
They lead forth the fame of their father; they weave together excellent glories; they are the possessors of wealth.
By means of qualities;
the quality has the mark as its cause.
Thus.

Furthermore, it is thus: that which is dead must certainly not be touched by the ascetic (*viku*) for the sake of protecting his son and disciples; otherwise, he incurs sin. For if the son is brought into the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) away from the boundary of propriety (*maryādā*), it is improper; having performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for him, even though the end was intended to be auspicious, it is certain that the father will fall into the world of hell (*nirayaloka*). He is swallowed by the abyss of the power of Yama; he is devoured by the fire of the child’s transgression. Such is the teacher regarding the conduct of the disciple.

[VS_14j§2] Even though one is an elder (*pantən*), he may still be in the realm of Yama; this is why a monk (*saṅ viku*) must never fail to exert effort. One must observe his *saṃskāra*, his conduct, his behavior, his observance of rules, and his adherence to the *brata* of the Holy One (*saṅ hyaṅ*). Furthermore, one must observe whether he is capable of performing the rites and rituals of the Holy One who dwells among men, as well as his lineage. One must never fail to respect the monk, nor fail to respect the elder. Even though he is an elder, his *saṃskāra*—his discipline and his rank—is such that even a person of high refinement who acts in that manner cannot easily find a place on the soil of Java. If that is so, it is for this reason that the monk must strive to ensure his fitness for *saṃsāra*, so that he may attain the supreme state (*uttamapada*). For even if one is a grandson or great-grandson of a refined person, it is not certain that he will be able to maintain the *brata* of the Holy One. Moreover, even if his conduct is observed to be refined in every way, and his *saṃskāra* is perfected, there may be a cause for his downfall. This is why the punishment is six *su* and four *ma*; this is the teaching of the masters (*mpuṅku*) together with their disciples, the venerable teachers (*bhaṭāra guru*), and furthermore, the correction of the monk toward his disciples, so that they do not fall away from what is required for their *saṃskāra*. This is because there are many causes for the smiles, gestures, and facial expressions of people.

[VS_14j§3] It is an error on the part of the one who performs the consecration (*saṃskāra*) if, while becoming a monk (*viku*), he causes the disciple to err. He must not comfort him; he must not release him from his duties there. Whether it be the Guru, the Guru’s wife, or the Guru’s son, they must all be treated with respect. One should not comfort them because they are deemed unfit; let him not act in such a manner. For in the midst of this, there is no cooling down from the teaching (*śāsana*) and logic (*yukti*); it contradicts the sacred scriptures (*śāstrāgama*). He must not comfort the disciple out of worldly affection, nor release the disciple out of a surge of anger. His purpose is solely to remain focused upon the state of the Blessed One’s sovereignty (*kabhujaṅga*). The meaning of this is that he merely cultivates stainless knowledge (*nirmalajñāna*).

[VS_14j§4] Now, regarding that expiation: the news is this. What is the direct perception? Its appearance is as follows: the established doctrine (siddhānta) is that one who drinks liquor, one who eats the flesh of a cow, a priest who commits the murder of a Brahmin (brahmahatyā), one who violates the bed of his teacher (gurutalpaka), and a thief—these constitute the characteristics of the murder of a Brahmin according to the venerable scripture.
A fool, a woman, a pregnant woman, a cow, a Brahmin woman, a Brahmin, a king, a teacher, and a sacrificer—by killing these, one is considered a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā). ||15||

[VS_15j§1] Regarding the Kaliṅga: a person who kills a cow, or a cow within the interior of a tree; a person who kills an ant, a bull, a Brāhmaṇī woman, or a Brāhmaṇa; a king, and so forth, including those who have been lords; an initiated teacher (ācārya-dīkṣita); or a sacrificer (yajamāna) who is a priest (viku) performing worship—such is the killing of a Brāhmaṇa (brahmahatyā).

[VS_15j§2] What is considered *bhrūṇahatyā* (the killing of an embryo)? It is when a person kills a child within the womb. That is *bhrūṇahatyā*, and it is even more severe than other [sins]. The sin of that person is the extreme *pātaka* (heinous crime) of *brahmahatyā* (the killing of a Brahmin). [The text] is somewhat obscure; let it be clarified by the venerable monk (*saṅ viku*). In brief, the venerable monk [says]: one must never kill unintentionally. Even if one is a follower (*śrāvaka*) of a person, one must never kill another human being unintentionally, provided they are innocent.

[VS_15j§3] Having fallen, there are the *ṅa*, *aṅrabyani*, *ibu*, *nini*, *bibī*, *sānak*, *kaponakan*, *mantu*, *kavalvan*, *ipen*, the wife of the elder brother (*rabiniṅ paman*), the wife of the elder brother-in-law (*rabiniṅ rāma tuha*), the wife of the younger brother-in-law (*rabiniṅ sapaṅalapan*), *varaṅ*, the elder brother-in-law (*rāma tuha*), the wife of the younger brother-in-law (*rabiniṅ kaponakan*), the wife of the younger brother (*rabiniṅ mantu*), and the wife of the younger brother (*rabiniṅ vvaṅ sānak*). These are the terms according to the *Āgama*.

[VS_15j§4] One who violates the Guru’s bed (*gurutaḷpaga*) is one who has sexual intercourse with the wife of the Guru, whether she be a woman of noble birth or a low-born woman, or the Guru’s daughter, or the Guru’s sister, or the Guru’s female slave, or others such as those who are not women, or even those who have taken possession of the Guru’s property. Even if there is no desire arising from the Guru, if one has sexual intercourse with the Guru’s wife or property, how can he be considered equal? This is not appropriate for the Guru, who merely enjoys the respectful service of his disciple; it is not permissible to conceal it.
The teacher read [the *ampunan*], and the disciple offered it to him; thus, the teacher’s transgression was expiated by the disciple in that manner.

[VS_15j§5] One may strike a woman who protects her teacher, whether she be a daughter, a granddaughter, a daughter-in-law, or a member of his lineage, or even a slave-girl. This is provided that the teacher has no affection for his pupil; he should discipline the pupil as a means of bestowing the teacher’s grace. This is for the mutual benefit of both teacher and pupil, so that the pupil may become disciplined and not commit the sin of violating the teacher’s bed. Such is the sequence.

[VS_15j§6] "Kill! O disciple, you have committed a fault out of fear of punishment; it was caused by your own arrogance, for your heart is full of defects. Again and again, the deer flees from the hunter because of its own fault, not because of the power of the trap. It is the same with the disciple who is extremely ill-behaved. Such a disciple is utterly self-willed; even when they bring forth their own faulty conduct, the teacher must not fail to forgive them. Rather, the teacher should offer satisfaction to that disciple, honoring the venerable teacher’s feet along with witnesses, offerings, and the sequence of ritual procedures."

Furthermore, what is the fault of that? It is repeatedly insulting one’s own teacher. If one acts in such a manner, it is well known that I am a *pantən*; indeed, such a person is called a *gurutalpaga* (one who violates the bed of the teacher).

[VS_15j§8] Theft (*steya*) consists of: taking what has not been given (*amakāvak*), stealing (*maliṅ*), pilfering (*manayab*), taking what is forgotten (*maṅutil*), taking what is hidden (*amələgandaṅ*), taking what is left behind (*aṅəntal*), taking what is placed down (*manumpuṅ*), taking the wife of another (*amuṅpaṅ strīniṅ len*), and seizing property (*ambaranaṅ*). This is theft.

[VS_15j§9] What, then, is the sixfold *ātatāyin*? There are nine types; they are as follows: one who steals the sandals (*anluh*), one who steals the staff (*maṅupas*), one who steals the mouth-cloth (*aṅamuk*), one who steals the water-strainer (*amurugul*), one who steals the sacred thread (*anunvani*), and one who steals the master’s belongings (*amiśunākən*). These are the six *ātatāyins*. All of them are not permitted to be purified by the Guru; there is no further expiation for them. Such a person is like a serpent; thus says the scripture (*āgama*) regarding one whose vows are broken. His fault is equal to that of the master, because such a mendicant causes the ruin of the kingdom. He does not possess the conduct of a wise man (*paṇḍita*). This is why the Guru must abandon his disciple who has seized his moral discipline (*śīla-yukti*), so that he may attain the totality and the partlessness, grasp what is auspicious, and reach the state that is beyond distinction (*aviśeṣa-pada*), possessing the supreme secret of knowledge. Such is the conduct of a mendicant. Furthermore, he must never lack enthusiasm for the sequence of the bathing ritual (*snānavidhikrama*), for so it is stated in the scripture.
The fire-related, the water-related, the Brahma-related, the wind-related, the mental, and the earth-related: bathing is said to be of these six kinds. 16.

[VS_16j] What? "The sixfold bath that is practiced," said the Paṇḍita. Its forms are as follows: Āgneya, Vāruṇa, Brāhmya, Vāyavya, Mānasa, and Pārthiva. Such are its six forms; one should apply oneself to them with effort.

Bathing with ashes is the fire-related (āgneya) bath; bathing in water is the water-related (vāruṇa) bath; bathing with mantras is the Brahmic (brāhmya) bath; and bathing with the dust raised by cows is the wind-related (vāyavya) bath. 17.

The *āgneya* bath has as its characteristic ash; furthermore, the *vāruṇa* bath has as its characteristic water. The *brāhmya* bath has as its characteristic mantras; furthermore, the *vāyavya* bath has as its characteristic the rubbing of the body from the head downwards, starting from the armpits up to the crown of the head, using fragrant substances mixed with pure water.
The recitation of mantras is the mental bath, while the worship at the three junctions of the day constitutes the ritual service;
touching the earth from a full sacred bathing site is called the earthly bath. 18.

[VS_18j] What is mental bathing? It consists of the characteristics of reciting mantras during the three daily rites (*trisandhyopāsana*) performed at dawn. Furthermore, what is earthly bathing? It is characterized by the water of sacred pilgrimage sites (*puṇyatīrtha*). Such are the forms of the sixfold bathing; let the ascetic (*viku*) take note of them.
One who has bathed in knowledge is the supreme "bathed" one; one is also "bathed" through observances and vows. Yet, one is not truly "bathed" if one does not proceed having bathed with ashes.

[VS_19j§1] Who? He who has bathed his head in the forest—that is, he who has bathed in the *vidyā* (sacred knowledge) of the Lord. His bath is that which is without signs (*animitta*) and serves as the purifier (*pavitra*) of the noble one; it is that which, having been established within the heart-lotus (*hṛdayakamala*), thereafter flows forth. There is he who possesses the bath of the observances and vows (*niyamavrata*); this is the ascetic (*viku*) who does not bathe with water.
Indeed, these ashes alone are the excellence of all ablutions.
That which has been eaten unknowingly while mixed with hair or insects, or that which is sprinkled with ashes and consecrated by speech—such food is blameless for sages. 20.

[VS_20j] What? It is that which is eaten; namely, insects, excrement, and hair. "Insects" refers to creatures such as those found in filth, in the head, on the body, or in the ears, and so forth—living beings that are subtle and impure. "Hair" refers to the hair of the head; it is not noticed during the consumption of all food because of its subtlety. There is no fault for the ascetic (viku) regarding that which he eats, provided he does not eat it intentionally. He does not avoid it because of its purity, due to the purifying power of the ashes and the water used by the ascetic, as well as his daily practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). Herein lies the scriptural authority: (Note: The Sanskrit source text for this section is *Vaiśeṣikasūtra* 6.18–21.)
One should burn away defects through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and sin through concentrations (dhāraṇā);
one should withdraw the sense-objects through withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and the non-divine qualities through meditation (dhyāna). 21. cd–ef.

[VS_21j] Prāṇāyāma removes defects; dhāraṇā removes afflictions; pratyāhāra removes sense objects; dhyāna eliminates qualities that are not conducive to excellence. This is the method of cultivation for the practitioner, as stated in the scriptures.
Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this is the tenfold characteristic of dharma.
[VS_22j] Retention is the state within the heart.
Patience (kṣamā) is the pacification of anger.
Self-restraint is the power of the intellect.
Non-stealing is not a stain upon me.
Purity consists of sipping water (ācamana), bathing with ashes (bhasmasnāna), and so forth.
The restraint of the senses is not for one who has not mastered the senses.
Hrīṃ ṅa iraṅ.
The knowledge is not manifold.
That which is true is false.
I have no anger; I am free from anger. These are all my ten dharmas.
Purity, sacrifice, austerity, charity, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ, observances, fasting, silence, and bathing—these are the ten rules (niyamas). 23.
[VS_23j] Purity is not constant; there is no ritual sipping of water for one who is perpetually impure.
I am the eternal sacrifice, the worshipful one.
Asceticism consists of the mind,
the body, and the senses.
I have no gift.
The recitation of one's own study is for the purpose of removing the various mental afflictions.
The restraint of the genitals is not performed by the penis.
I have taken this vow for the sake of the fleshless [state].
Fasting means being without food.
I am silent,
having risen above [all].
Bathing, the daily recitation, and so forth—these are its ten components; these are what are called the *niyamas*.
Compassion, forbearance, truthfulness, non-violence, self-restraint, uprightness, meditation, serenity, sweetness, and gentleness—these are the ten *yamas*. 24.
[VS_24j] Compassion is not praise for you.
Patience is the pacification of anger.
It is true that I am not weary.
Non-violence is not something to be disregarded.
Self-restraint is the power of the intellect.
straightforwardness (emended from *sārjava* to *ārjava*)
5) My intellect is not proficient.
In meditation,
I contemplate the true nature of the Lord.
May I have confidence.
Sweetness is not tasted by the mind; it is experienced by the mind through the senses.
Gentleness is not something that can be grasped; all of these together number ten, and thus they are called *yama*.
Those twice-born who recite the ten stations of the Dharma, and having studied them, live in accordance with them, go to the supreme goal. ||25||

[VS_25j] Who? He who has destroyed the mind of the twice-born (dvijāti) regarding the states of the ten dharmas; he is the one who has transcended them. He has realized the ten dharmas; he has attained the supreme goal (paramagati), having reached the state of the divine beings (saṅ hyaṅ kabhujaṅgan). This is the most excellent Lord Maheśvara, worthy of being served.
Truth, vows, or even asceticism—all that is useless toward those who are satisfied with knowledge, free from desire, and whose lives are inherently peaceful. ||26||

[VS_26j§1] What? It is the vow (vrata) of the Gavayaka. Its types are as follows: the *sāttvika* of the sword, which is the worship of flowers; the *sāttvika* of wakefulness, which is the worship of lamps; and the *sāttvika* of knowledge, which is the worship of praise. Furthermore, there is that which is practiced by the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*), namely the asceticism (*tapas*). As for what that tranquility (*kaśānta*) is, all those vows of asceticism have heaven (*svarga*) as their fruit. The very happiness of the mind is what is cultivated through the practice of those vows of asceticism, along with all the various forms of suffering. However, whatever the fruit of those vows of asceticism may be, if it is such, it is evil (*pāpa*). Thus spoke Lord Maheśvara. One must strive diligently. 0 ||
[VS_26j§2] Thus spoke the Lord Śaṅkara, the most excellent of heroes:
[VS_27s-ab] Just as the radiance of the sun and the moon is equal by day and by night, [VS_27s-cd] so too is the gait of the mendicant; his heart is not devoid [of that same equanimity]. ||27||

[VS_27j§1] What? It is the smallness of equanimity (*samatā*). How does one become small? This is the illustration: just as the venerable deities Candra and Āditya illuminate the entire world—both the stationary and the moving, the low, the middling, and the superior, the good and the bad, pleasure and pain, the pure and the mixed—they purify all with their rays; there is no spot on their bodies that cannot be touched. In this same way, O ascetic, you must become small. Do not be conceited about your knowledge and your manifold virtues; do not be defiled by the three impurities (*trimala*): *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Thus spoke Lord Śaṅkara: "One must strive for the Self."
[VS_27j§2] O Lord Śambhu, please destroy these excellent boars.
[VS_28s-ab] One who eats excrement, impurity, filth, and even feces; [VS_28s-cd] and one who consumes ashes and liquor—having done that, he incurs sin. ||28||

[VS_28j§1] What? One must not exert effort toward the instruments (upākaraṇa) of the Lord. Such as ashes, a water-pot, a rosary, a conch shell, and a water-strainer. One must not speak while holding them; or rather, when drinking from the skin bag (tvak kunaṅ), so that one does not commit the sin of spilling. Thus spoke Lord Śambhu. One should strive for self-restraint. 0 ||
[VS_28j§2] O Lord Rudra, listen to these efforts:
[VS_29s-ab] Non-violence, celibacy, truthfulness that is not for worldly transaction, and non-stealing—these five are the *yamas* proclaimed by Rudra. ||29||
[VS_29j§1] What is it?

It is non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) toward all living beings. This is indeed the birth of a human being; this is the fruit of that reasoning. There is no other means of purification than this. Thus it is said: "He alone is a true ascetic (*viku*) who does not cause harm."
[VS_29j§2] Now, regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*):

I am a practitioner of the holy life who has not yet mastered the recitation of the mantra *oṃ saba tā ai*. Such is my status as a practitioner of the holy life. There are three types of practitioners of the holy life: namely, the black practitioner of the holy life (*kṛṣṇabrahmacārī*), the variegated practitioner of the holy life (*śavalabrahmacārī*), and the white practitioner of the holy life (*śuklabrahmacārī*). These are its three forms.

The *kṛṣṇabrahmacārī* does not die with his body; he abandons his physical form. Furthermore, he does not undergo rebirth. He has mastered *dhyāna*, *yoga*, *japa*, and *samādhi*. This is what is meant by being a *kṛṣṇabrahmacārī*.

The *śabalabrahmacārī* does not observe the rules of conduct (*māna*) nor the fasts (*piṅrva* and *piṅtiga*). He attains this state whenever the time is right—whether on ordinary days or during sacred festivals (*parvan*). Indeed, he abandons all that his children might desire; for him, *kevalya*, *yoga*, *japa*, and *samādhi* are present at all times. Therefore, he is called a *śabalabrahmacārī*.

[VS_29j§5] What is meant by a "pure celibate" (*śuklabrahmacārī*)? It is one who is entirely free from attachment toward women; who does not gaze at them with longing; and who does not become infatuated with women in emptiness (*śūnya*). Even if there are many mothers, sisters, or female friends, he does not look upon them with desire. He causes his mind to set [into tranquility] through meditation (*dhyāna*), yoga, recitation (*japa*), and concentration (*samādhi*). Such is the pure celibate; this is the essence of the life of celibacy.
Truth is indeed truth, O wise one! It is manifested in one’s appearance, in one’s speech, in one’s conduct, and in one’s observance of vows; it is that by which the noble person is recognized.
That which is beyond conventional discourse is not characterized by conventional discourse. Why is that? Because it is not subject to the defects of deficiency.
Non-stealing (asteya).
What is non-stealing?
Its characteristic is as follows: its characteristic is this, namely:

The doer, the one who causes others to act, the enjoyer, the director, the one who points out the place, the protector, the knower, and the guardian—these are remembered as the eight types of thieves. (30)

[VS_30j§1] What? Truly, what is the nature of stealing? It is: plotting, plotting together, giving food, giving shelter, providing cover, providing tools for stealing, and inciting others. These are called the eight thieves; you must not harbor them, O monk. This is called the vow of Yama: "O Lord Rudra, may you pierce through my very self."
[VS_30j§2] O Lord Śiva, please explain this further.
[VS_31s-ab] Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food, and vigilance—these five are the *niyamas* proclaimed by Śiva. ||31||
[VS_31j§1] What? Absence of anger.
Why? Because it destroys the dust of passion. Do not be impulsive in speech; do not be impulsive in action.
[VS_31j§2] Service to the teacher with devotion is not toward one who is not a teacher; this is the nature of another teacher.
It is recorded that there are those who are advanced in age, advanced in austerity, and advanced in knowledge; among these,
the one advanced in age is to be honored.
V. Today is my birthday;
it is like the beginning of a new year.
Therefore, let there be both the preparation of offerings and the giving of instruction.
"I am not one who has grown old through asceticism, nor am I one devoted to the practice of penance."

I am one who has grown old in wisdom, yet I have no attachment to the Lord. In brief, my only concern is for those whom the Lord accepts; indeed, you yourself are such a person. This is my devotion toward my guru.

[VS_31j§3] Purity is not characterized by constant impurity. It consists of eating [only] what is not stale, bathing constantly, avoiding the sun, using ashes, sandalwood, and the water of Śiva together with the *vevasa* [garment]. Regarding purity through mantra: *oṃ sabatāi*.

[VS_31j§4] There is no need for the lightness of food that does not satisfy even when one encounters delicious flavors; do not be attached to enjoyments such as meat. Be moderate toward all living beings; contentment alone is sufficient for you.
Heedfulness is not merely to avoid what is forbidden;
it is also to follow that which is enjoined by the teacher.
[VS_31j§6] Indeed, that is not the *niyama* vow; such is the sign of Lord Śiva. That which is the *yama-niyama* vow has ten components in its total number; these are what are known as the *daśaśīla*.
On earth, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) acts as an obstacle;
in hell, it is like a fierce fire.
In the immediate counting of the female attendants of the Gaṇas, there is a penalty of a hundredfold fault.
For whoever does not protect the Pāśupata conduct, [he is not a true follower]. [VS_32s-d]

[VS_32j] Regarding the meaning: a practitioner who does not exert himself in the five trainings and ten precepts lacks the sacred implements of Śiva. It is evident that he has not awakened his own nature within the cavity [of the heart]. Now, as for the nature of those sacred implements of Śiva which serve as ornaments for the practitioner: the *yajñasūtra* together with the *savita*, the *bhasma*, the *gaṇitrī*, and the water vessel. As for this *yajñasūtra*:

As for that person who is a twice-born ascetic (*dvija-vratatung*), if he does not guard his moral conduct (*śīla*), he will be reborn in the realm of Yama; however, if he does guard his moral conduct, it becomes his path to the state of Lord Īśvara. Likewise, as for that ash-smeared ascetic (*bhasma-saṅviku*), if he does not guard his moral conduct, he will be reborn in the realm of Yama;
but if he guards his moral conduct, it becomes his radiance, shining constantly day and night, both for himself and others. Thus it is.
Calculator; counting board; abacus.

The ascetic (viku) has become a calculator of time; he has become the instrument for the cutting of time (death), which is the limb of this [world] of defects. How many years have passed since he was initiated? He is one year old in the calculation of time, provided his conduct (śīla) is not protected. But if his conduct is protected, he becomes a jewel of gems (maṇiratna) possessing all qualities, which yields all fruits and bestows blessings at all times. That is the equipment of the ascetic; it grants heaven and liberation, provided his conduct is protected. But if his conduct is not protected, he becomes a cow, a buffalo, a dog, a monkey, or a wild beast, being roasted at all times. That is why one must never fail to obey the word of the Guru, for he is renowned as the most excellent among those who are appropriate [to serve]. That is why we ask you for the teacher’s fee (gurudakṣiṇā), so that there may be no stumbling in your actions, and that you and we may be well. Thus spoke Lord Paśupati. One should strive to understand this, together with the words of the Śāstra.
Anger, greed, and delusion are known as passion and hatred;
all these five enemies reside within one's own body. 33.

[VS_33j] What? There are five enemies residing within the body. Such is their nature. Herein is the sequence of the five enemies: anger (*krodha*), greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), passion (*rāga*), and hatred (*dveṣa*). Such are the five enemies within the body. One must be vigilant against them, O ascetic (*viku*), for when they reach their full growth, they cause ruin. Why is that? [VS_34s-ab] Turbidity, deceit, folly, cruelty, reviling, and hypocrisy;
[VS_34s-cd] Falsehood, envy, and violence—these are all fourteen, five times four. //34//

[VS_34j§1] What? The faults (*sasaṅa*) are fourteen in number. Which are those faults? They are: impurity (*kaluṣa*), deceit (*dhūrta*), folly (*mūrkha*), cruelty (*krūra*), censure (*ninda*), hypocrisy (*dambha*), falsehood (*mithyā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and violence (*hiṃsā*). These are the nine that arise; they dwell within the body. Therefore, one should guard against them; let the ascetic (*viku*) not be negligent, but strive to maintain his conduct (*śīla*).
[VS_34j§2] Abandon, O Liṅga, this attachment to the sacred scriptures; that is what the venerable ascetic must do.
[VS_35s-ab] Attachment to women, drinking, and gambling; attachment to hunting and calling out; [VS_35s-cd] attachment to sleep, mountains, houses, solitude, food, and water. ||35||
Attached to women,
one does not know the true nature of union.
One addicted to drinking wine does not know what to drink; one addicted to gambling [does not know what to play].
I am one who has never played at dice.
He was addicted to hunting and became frantic.
I am not one who is attached to invitations or to the sight of spectacles.
I, attached to sleep,
do not know anything.
The one attached to the mountain is not aware of the height of the mountain.
One who is attached to the household does not know what is truly delightful in the home.
One who is attached to emptiness does not know the stain of the self.
One who is attached to food does not know what is truly delicious.
clinging to water; attached to water; immersed in water.

I know what is beautiful in water—such as springs, lakes, waterfalls, rivers, the Narmadā, the Gaṅgā, the Sarayū, and the ocean—and all that is beautiful in stone, which is indeed a source of delight; yet all these are seized by the enemy of the Lord of Yogins. All the objects of the senses in this world are the cause for which a practitioner (*viku*) must not indulge in sense-objects, lest he fall from his status as a Lord of Yogins. Furthermore, O practitioner, if you desire to attain the state of the Lord (*īśa*), you must possess knowledge alone; through it, the state of Śiva will become manifest and attainable, so that you shall abide in the knowledge of the partless (*niṣkalajñāna*).
Furthermore, as for that which was previously empty of words, it has dissolved into his very essence; from that, he takes birth among humans. And what is the nature of his birth as a human?
[VS_36s-a] A man who is of noble birth, handsome, virtuous, wealthy, illustrious, and ascetic;
[VS_36s-b] one who has mastered the sciences, intelligent, pure-minded, meritorious, endowed with forbearance and fortitude; [VS_36s-c] one who is generous, fortunate, and an enjoyer of prosperity.
Now, that Dharma of accomplished fame is the protector;
he is the partless yogi who, through the three pledges, pervades the abode of Īśa throughout birth.

[VS_36j§1] Who is he? He is one who possesses union with that which is called the *śivapada*. Even so, it is not merely that his yoga bears fruit—such as the fruits of *homa* and so forth—but rather, throughout his successive births, he becomes a cause for the growth of the Threefold Rule (*trisamaya*). He is born as a human being; he possesses majesty within the world, beginning with noble lineage, followed by handsome form and excellent character. He is favored by Fortune (*śrī*), and he possesses great power, for he is an ascetic (*tapasvī*). Such is the nature of this man: he has mastered the sciences (*vidyāpāraga*), he knows how to study all treatises (*sarvaśāstra*), he is intelligent and wise, and his mind is auspicious and his intellect is refined. He is meritorious (*puṇya*) and his speech is pure; he is not fickle or restless. He is patient, his tranquility is profound, and he is steadfast. He is exceedingly brave, generous, free from craving for wealth and life, fortunate, and holds all that is good in the world. He enjoys happiness, is beloved by all, and is wealthy, possessing gold and silver. His fame is great, and he is righteous, knowing the sublime Dharma. He is well-protected and protects all his subjects; he is a friend who knows how to cherish his allies, and his circle of kinsmen is beyond reproach. Furthermore, if there is a human being such as this, he is a vessel for birth; when he dies, he returns to the state of Rudra, because he has produced the status of a Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*). One should recognize that such a person is manifestly the venerable Rudra himself; he is indeed a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). ||0||

Thus is the instruction for those observing the vows (*vrati*). One must not be ignorant regarding that which the *viku* (priest) has taught; one must know it. One must know the five precepts (*pañcaśikṣā*) and the ten moralities (*daśaśīla*). Such is the sequence, O noble one (*bhujaṅga*): one must not fail to pay homage; one must not fail to show respect; one must not fail to remain humble. One must not be ignorant of how to eat, nor of how to drink; one must not be ignorant of what is fit to be consumed; one must not be ignorant of what is fit to be drunk. One must choose one’s food; one must choose one’s drink; one must choose the manner of one’s speech. One must not be ignorant of the consideration of time and place. Such is the sequence, O noble one, regarding his knowledge within the lineage of Brahmā (*brahmavaṃśa*). There exists a scriptural passage (*liṅga*) concerning this.
[VS_37s-ab] Those who have passed away from their own duties, subsisting on the labor of others;
[VS_37s-cd] those Brahmins who disregard their status as twice-born and behave like Śūdras. ||37||

[VS_37j§1] What is it? It is when a person lives by his own karma and makes a livelihood from it, yet he does not maintain the dignity that is the source of another person’s conduct, such as a Brāhmaṇa. Although a Brāhmaṇa is the foremost among the twice-born (*dvijāti*), he has sunk into the conduct of a Śūdra; that which serves as his means of subsistence is what causes him to lose his status as a twice-born. There are indeed some *vipras* who are like this: they are just like Śūdras, even down to being *caṇḍālas*, because their behavior is caused by that of a Śūdra.

[VS_37j§2] If one does not understand that, it is a transgression for him, O Serpent, due to the lack of *saṃskāra*. The punishment for his Highness is as follows: for a person who understands but does not perform the consecration (*dīkṣā*) for him, if the disciple does not succeed in accordance with his venerable instruction on the observances (*vratiśāsana*), the *saṃskāra* must be performed for him. There is indeed a limit to the *saṃskāra* for such a person: the punishment is three *suvarṇas* and two *māṣakas* for one who has been consecrated together with others; the punishment is one *suvarṇa* and four *māṣakas* for one who understands the venerable instruction on the observances but does not perform his own *saṃskāra*. For one who understands the teacher’s collective assembly, he must exert effort. Thus ends the instruction on the observances (*vratiśāsana*). End. 0.
Appendix: The Text of the *Ga* Lontar

Sharada Rani: We have provided the text of *ka*, *kha*, and *gha* above. However, the root verses of the *ga* lontar differ in each instance starting from verse 4; therefore, this text is presented here separately as an appendix. Important variant readings are indicated here and there by writing "lo. within parentheses. The specific variant readings of the Sanskrit verses have already been provided above in the main text. For the sake of convenience, the numbering of the main text has been appended to these verses. In the present text, the sixteenth verse does not appear at all. Following the twenty-fifth verse, there is one additional verse not found in the main text; to indicate it, we have numbered it 25ka. From verse 25 onward, the main text extends up to verse 37, whereas in the present text, the conclusion occurs precisely at 25ka. The extant text, though brief, is generally very well-organized.
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, abstention from worldly affairs, and vigilance— these five are the observances (niyamas) spoken by Śiva.

[VS_appendix-04j§1] Non-anger (*akrodha*): what is anger? It is the failure to serve one’s guru. Its cause is that one does not revere the excellent, the excellent guru. Purity (*śauca*): it is constant purity and worship of the Lord. Non-worldliness (*avyavahārika*): it is not being worldly. Heedfulness (*apramāda*): it is not neglecting the practice of the noble *kabhujaṅga*. The threefold *kalima* is the *niyamavrata*, as stated by the Lord Śiva.

[VS_appendix-04j§2] The suffixes *ikan* and *anaṅ* are not applied to *yamavrata*. One must protect that vow; the practitioner (*viku*) must proceed with great care. For if one does not guard it, the mind will surely become wavering. It is evident that if one strays from the path of the wise, such a person will end up consuming what is unfit to be eaten, drinking what is unfit to be drunk, and approaching women who should not be approached—even if they are one's own mother. This is the lowest of the low.

[VS_appendix-04j§3] For one who observes the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsāvrata*), anger, delusion, intoxication, pride, and envy are causes of harm; likewise, desire is a cause of harm to various degrees. There are two types of desire: that which is internal and that which is external. Furthermore, there is no fault for one who commits violence for the sake of *dharma*. There is no fault in killing for the sake of worshiping the gods, the ancestors, guests, or spirits. Such violence is not considered a transgression. Regarding sacrificial animals (*pituvi*) that are permitted to be killed—such as goats, sheep, and buffaloes—they do not experience suffering; therefore, they are not considered victims of violence. One should understand the nature of their death accordingly.

Furthermore, there are cases where killing is not considered a transgression. Its forms are: wild animals, birds, fish, and aquatic creatures; even if one kills many of them while wandering about, it is no fault for the ascetic (*viku*) to kill them. Moreover, there are those who are fit to be killed: those devoid of Dharma and devoid of Yoga; the causes of bodily corruption. Their forms are: snakes, scorpions, and centipedes; these are the causes of bodily corruption. It is fitting for the ascetic to kill them if they enter his dwelling, or if they enter the house of a friend or relative of his; even if they subsequently enter the house of his teacher, it is no fault for the ascetic to kill them. There may be a murderer on the path, lurking and hiding, or attacking and pursuing the ascetic; if the ascetic kills him, it is no fault, for such an act is called self-protection. However, there are wicked people who are deceitful and unfit for the ascetic to kill, because there is no danger from their bodies; it is improper for the ascetic to kill such persons.

[VS_appendix-04j§5] Or suppose there is a woman who is hostile toward her husband, her children, or her siblings; yet, because of her great intelligence, she remains patient with them. She does not harbor malice toward them, even when they mistreat her. If she were to mistreat them, it would be improper for her to act thus. This is because she is one who possesses the mark of fearlessness; she is not at fault for being mistreated. Furthermore, if there is a woman of immoral character, or perhaps her daughter, and they both behave wickedly toward their husbands, yet she herself does not behave wickedly—if she were to behave wickedly, it would be improper for her to act thus. Or, if her husband is of such a nature that he is prone to violence, then her behaving wickedly is merely a response to his violence. Whether it is the woman or her daughter who behaves wickedly, she is not at fault for acting in that way.

[VS_appendix-04j§6] It is appropriate that the killer (*hiṃsaka*) be the cause of death; therefore, he is the one who dies. This is fitting. However, if it were otherwise, there would be no fault in the one who dies, for there is no movement in what has been destroyed, nor is there motion. Furthermore, the fruit of action (*karmaphala*) is not ultimately linked to the sound of the voice. Yet, he is extremely fickle; he does not remain still toward the killer. It is fitting that he is thus, for it is not proper to subject him to ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*), because there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for what is deemed "fitting" (*pantən*). For this reason, the ascetic (*viku*) must never fail to exert effort in guarding the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsāvrata*); this is first among those who observe the vow of self-restraint (*yamavrata*).

[VS_appendix-04j§7] What is *brahmacarya*? It is not knowing women. What is its form? It is as follows: the white *brahmacārī*, the variegated *brahmacārī*, and the black *brahmacārī*. One who does not know women even while living with those who serve his teacher—having this as the motive for turning away from worldly desires, for generating service to the teacher, and for desiring to master the sacred sciences (*śāstra*) of the gods and humans, namely logic (*tarka*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*)—if that ascetic (*viku*) has no other wife than the one he married when entering the householder stage, and does not take another wife thereafter, he is the black *brahmacārī*.

[VS_appendix-04j§8] Who is the *śabalabrahmacārī* (the impure celibate)? He is one who serves his teacher like a woman, or serves his teacher like a householder; he desires the increase of offspring, yet he knows that the lineage will not flourish. His wife is many, yet she is no wife; he has no son, though he knows the time for sexual union. Whatever is auspicious regarding sexual union, at that time he conceals the act of union; he does not take pleasure in the union itself. Because of this, he understands the evil nature of the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*), for when one is attached to women, it becomes the fault of desire (*kāma*). Desire produces anger; anger produces greed; it produces delusion (*moha*); it produces intoxication (*mada*); it produces envy (*mātsarya*). Thus, the objects of the senses are truly false. The more one indulges in women, the more one is pulled by the attachment to women. One's intellect becomes confused; it leads to the violation of another’s wife by a monk, the approach of those who should not be approached (*agamya*), the approach of the teacher’s wife (*gurvaṅganā*), and the approach of those who are unapproachable. To take as a wife one who is unfit to be a wife—such as a sister, a daughter, a granddaughter, a female relative, a female cousin, or a niece—this constitutes the "approach of those who should not be approached" (*agamya-gamana*). Taking another man’s wife as one’s own wife is "another’s wife" (*paradāra*). Such people do not deserve to reach the world of bliss (*nirayaloka*); they are swallowed by the pit by the forces of Yama. Such is the "approach of those who should not be approached. Its sin is even greater. It is not easy to escape from the pit of the god Yama. Once one has emerged from the pit, one’s life is miserable, like a scorched insect, a lizard, a cricket, a cicada, a grasshopper, or a cricket—all such things are its miserable state. Furthermore, the sin of approaching the teacher’s wife is even greater. Its forms include: taking the teacher’s wife as one’s own wife, having sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife, [approaching] the teacher’s daughter, or even the teacher’s granddaughter. Such are the forms of approaching those who should not be approached. This is what is called "fallen" (*patita*). The transgression of a monk who acts in such a way is included within the category of the great sins (*pantən*). For this reason, the wise man must strive to protect his celibacy (*brahmacārya*). This is the second vow of the god Yama.

[VS_appendix-04j§9] What is truth? It is when I am true to the words of the ascetic (*viku*); one must strive to guard one's speech. One should not be untrue to one’s own word, for there are many disputants regarding the faults of speech. Furthermore, one must avoid harshness of speech; speak only what is pleasant. One should not utter words that are unwholesome. One must not speak words born of anger. One should not harbor malice or take oaths, for such things as malice and oaths are false speech. Moreover, truth also resides in conduct and in vows (*vrata*), for if an ascetic is not truthful regarding his vows, he is unworthy.

[VS_appendix-05-09j§1] What things are not to be eaten by one who observes the Siddhānta vows? Whatever is offered as a sacrificial oblation (*inuhutan*) is to be eaten by one who observes the Siddhānta vows. What are the animals that are not to be eaten? The elephant, the horse, the dog, the *puṣa* (jackal), the *kuvuk*, the *garaṅgaraṅan*, the *viṅsaṅ*, the *tikus*, the *ulā*, the *macan*, the *laṅkapa*, the *ruti*, the *tḍak*, the *galiṅ*, the *rathe*, the *vipra*, the *yutuṅ*, the *vuk*, the *virog*, the *viyuṅ*, the *tiṅkəl*, the *nīla*, the *badal*, the *kararap*, the *lalapa*, the *tken*, the *vulun*, and the *tuṅhin*. These are not to be eaten by one who observes the Siddhānta vows. Furthermore, those that are always to be eaten are the *krūra* and its like; all kinds of meat that have been cooked, such as *bibidho*, *dok*, *daryas*, *alapalap*, *trilaklak*, *cod*, *gagaṇḍan*, and the flesh of domestic fowl (*manuk viḍu*). These are not to be eaten. Furthermore, blue-winged birds, such as the crow, the *kak*, the *caṅkiluṅ*, and the *ṅūniṅūni* bird that makes human sounds, such as the *atat*, the *syuṅ*, and the *jalak*. Such are the examples of those that are not to be eaten.

[VS_appendix-05-09j§2] Furthermore, among the five-clawed animals (*pañcanakha*), some are edible while others are not fit to be eaten. Their types are as follows: the *varāha* (wild boar), the *laṇḍaka*, the *vayavaka*, and the *kūrma* (tortoise)—these are edible. However, those that are *bhūḥkṛmi* (earth-dwelling insects) and *prāṇikṛmi* (living insects) are not to be eaten. Their types include: *ulər*, *momahiṅ*, *lmah*, *kuti*, and so forth; these are not to be eaten. As for the *prāṇikṛmi*, their types are: *siṅgat*, *lalər*, *namuk*, *rəṅit*, *titiṅgi*, *tuma*, *kapiñjala*, *limpit*; these are not to be eaten by one who observes the *siddhāntavrata*. Likewise, the flesh of the *gomāṅsa*, *gavaya*, horse, *konta*, and donkey are not to be eaten. However, the cow and the *gavaya* are pure in their nature; their skin, if it has been used for travel, is not fit to be eaten. But as for what is eaten by one observing the *siddhānta*, the aforementioned meats are as follows: *varāha*, *laṇḍaka*, *kūrma*, *badavaṅ*, *bulus*, *baniṅ*, *pəñu*, *pḍok*, wild game, *varāha*, wild chicken, buffalo, sheep, *bañak*, *hitik*, *ḍara*, *tiṅgiliṅ*, *kidaṅ*, *bəmḍiśil*, *kañcil*, *mañjaṅan*—these are fit to be eaten by one observing the *siddhāntavrata*. Furthermore, regarding birds: apart from those previously mentioned as edible, such as the *mrak*, *kadaba*, *vantən*, *ijohan*, *vuruvuru*, *valivis*, *trabāyak*, *kalvaṅ*, and so forth, these are fit to be eaten. Regarding the shells of crabs (*ivak lvah*) and the shells of sea creatures (*ivak sāgar*), these are fit to be eaten provided they do not have a foul odor (*vuhaya*) and are not excessively hard (*atyanta riṅ gə̄ṅ*). However, large fierce fish (*mīna raudra*) are not to be eaten. Moreover, one who observes the *siddhānta* must not eat meat that has been cooked with onions (*surudan*), nor meat that has been cooked with garlic (*satumpaṅan camah*), nor meat from a *koṅkulan camah*. Furthermore, if it has been cooked with cats, chickens, or cocks, it is not to be eaten. Nor should one eat meat that has been cooked with *sitaṅśayan* or is impure, nor meat that has been touched by saliva. However, if one eats meat that has been cooked by one observing the *siddhāntavrata*, it is permissible. This constitutes "eating what is not to be eaten" (*abhakṣyabhakṣaṇa*). Likewise, there are things not to be drunk (*apeyapeya*). Their types are: drinking things that are unfit to be consumed, such as the bark of the *badeg*, the bark of the *layaṅ*, and the bark of the *budur*; these are not drunk by one observing the *siddhānta*. However, those that are drunk by one observing the *siddhāntavrata* are: *brəm* and Chinese honey (*madhu*). Furthermore, if there is a *siddhānta* that permits eating meat, the reason is that the person does not know [the prohibition]; such a person must perform penance (*prāyaścitta*). He must undergo penance before his preceptor (*saṅ guru*). If he is unable to perform penance, he is forbidden [from such acts]. Furthermore, if he eats meat due to the influence of delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), or intoxication (*mada*), this is forbidden. The consequence of this prohibition is that he may not be accepted by the venerable *Siddhāntaśāsana*; his adherence to the true vow (*kasatyavrata*) will perish. This is the third, the venerable *yamavrata*.

[VS_appendix-05-09j§3] He is not one who engages in worldly transactions (*avyāvahārika*). This is the rule: that which constitutes a worldly transaction for a *śramaṇa* (ascetic) is as follows: even if he possesses property such as land, children, cattle, or slaves—male and female—and his lineage, descendants, and further progeny, he remains non-transactional. However, it is a cause for reproach if he is excessively attached to the assistance provided by others. The implication regarding the property of a *śramaṇa* is this: if he possesses protection consisting of women, property, land, male and female slaves, sons, grandsons, and the succession of descendants, he is still non-transactional; yet he must also refrain from performing his own worldly actions (*svakarman*). He is fit to be non-transactional. But if a *śramaṇa* is non-transactional only in name, he does not fulfill his duty, because a *śramaṇa* has no business in buying and selling, nor in lending and borrowing. He is one who buys and sells, and he is one who lends and borrows. He exerts himself in buying and selling, and he exerts himself in lending and borrowing. There is no end to his involvement in trade and commerce, nor in all matters of debt and creditor. The implication is that there are many things fit for lending and borrowing, and likewise for buying and selling. That is why the *śramaṇa* himself must guard his vow of non-transactionality. This is the fourth divine vow, the *yamavrata*.

[VS_appendix-05-09j§4] Non-stealing (*asteya*). This is the precept for a practitioner (*sādhaka*): not to look at, nor to touch, nor to take, nor to seize, nor to covet another’s property. It is improper to act thus; one must not look upon cows, buffaloes, dogs, or any living being whatsoever during the day. Furthermore, such acts constitute a defilement (*punahsaṃskāra*), which is a transgression (*thar*).

What is the nature of stealing? Furthermore, what is the character of one who does not practice it? It is as follows: there is a monk who wanders from place to place on his journey. He has no provisions for the road; he carries ten *hantimun* [of rice], one *baligo*, and some *sagəgəm*. His path is through the forest; he eats his rice according to necessity. There are four *kaləvih* and four *tyuṅ* [measures]. When he travels, he carries boiled rice, *laṅsəb*, and *vuṅlvan*. If he stays overnight at a certain place, he must leave his belongings behind in the house. However, if he takes them with him from the house, his livelihood will be disturbed. Moreover, if he leaves them there, and they are lost or damaged, he commits theft. He is liable to be punished by those possessing wealth, even if he does not know the value of the goods. If he steals high-value items, he incurs sin; if he steals low-value items, he finds contentment. Therefore, one must guard against the vow of non-stealing. This is the fifth divine vow, the vow of non-stealing (*asteyavrata*).

[VS_appendix-05-09j§5] Abandon that restrictive vow. Non-anger is not what is called anger; it is when there is no enemy toward whom one becomes angry. There is a verse concerning this, its characteristic being as follows:
There is no friend equal to knowledge; there is no enemy equal to anger.
There is no affection equal to that for a son; there is no power greater than destiny.

[VS_appendix-10j§1] Therefore, do not disparage knowledge (*vidyā*), for it is the friend that leads one from this world to the supreme state. Furthermore, that which is not knowledge cannot be mastered through repeated practice of reasoning. Do not disparage anger as an enemy; it should not be suppressed. A hero slays an enemy who can be suppressed, but anger cannot be taken away. Because it does not enter the heart, all manifest purposes fail to be accomplished by it. The venerable Śrī Luṅhā said: "One who does not restrain anger is truly wretched. There is no love like that of a son, and there is no power like that of a god. Such is the meaning of the verse: "One should abandon anger," for its nature is such that if it is not destroyed, the vow of non-anger (*akrodhabrata*) will not be attained. First is the vow of self-restraint (*niyamabrata*).

[VS_appendix-10j§2] This is what is meant by service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*). It is being like-minded and not being unkind toward the teacher. For this reason, the teacher bestows the teaching of the *viku* (ascetic); the cause for this is that one does not attain *apavarga* (liberation). This is because if the teacher is negligent in his duties as a *viku*, it is not good for him to provide instruction on what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and what is to be adopted (*upadeśa*). This applies even regarding the five precepts (*pañcaśīla*) and the ten virtues (*daśadharma*), let alone regarding the profound teachings of the sacred *kriyā*. Thus, the path leading to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is lost; that is why such conduct must be avoided.
Service to the guru; this is the second auxiliary of yoga, namely the observance of rules and vows.

[VS_appendix-10j§3] What is purity (*śauca*)? It is constant purity and worship; always performing worship of Lord Śivāditya; auspiciously serving the Sun; auspiciously performing the sacred rites (*anuṣṭhāna*); applying ashes; reciting mantras (*japa*); and possessing the fortune to know the rules for ritual bathing (*snānavidhi*). Such is purity. This is the third sacred observance, the vow of restraint (*niyamavrata*).

[VS_appendix-10j§4] Lightness of diet (*āhāralāghava*) is contentment with what one eats. For if there were only pleasure for the ascetic, his mind would become agitated and restless; it is certain that if he consumes food that is heavy, impure, stolen, or unfit to be eaten, that becomes the cause of his lack of lightness in diet. This is the fourth divine observance (*niyamavrata*).

[VS_appendix-10j§5] Now, heedfulness (*apramāda*) is that which does not neglect the service of the Guru, nor what is manifest, nor what is unfit to be consumed. It consists of: *sarvārcana* (universal worship), *adhyāya* (study), *adhyāpaka* (teaching), *svādhyāya* (recitation), *vrata* (vow), meditation (*dhyāna*), yoga, and *śivārcana* (worship of Śiva). These constitute the beginning of universal worship. Their forms are as follows: offering various kinds of worship to the Lord; *yārcana* (worship of the way); *adhyāya*, called studying; *adhyāpaka*, called teaching; *svādhyāya*, called the recitation of the essence of what has been studied; *vrata*, called fasting and so forth; *dhyāna*, called contemplating the form of the Lord and the true nature of the Holy One who is worshipped by all the worlds; *yoga*, called breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth, as well as understanding the Holy One’s instruction and the path for attaining one's destiny. This applies to those who are qualified as ascetics (*viku*) as well as those who are not qualified as ascetics. They should not be overly concerned with writing or reading, nor with recitation, nor with debating back and forth when there is doubt regarding their conduct. If it is a means to achieve Dharma (*dharmasādhana*), they should be qualified; they should not have any fixed dwelling place. They should not go about constantly from house to house, begging. They should not be slaves, nor servants, nor beggars, nor hunters. Such are the things they should avoid being summoned for; let them not go there. Likewise, if they enter a house to beg, let them not depart empty-handed. Furthermore, they should not frequent places of gambling. They should have no great attachment, nor should they harbor resentment. This leads to misfortune and suffering.

*Tilamūrti: The Ritual of Initiation (Dīkṣāvidhi)* The venerable Upadeśa said: "O supreme Lord of Yogins, he who is not afflicted by the impurities of others nor by those of his own kin is fit to be a Guru. He must be capable of bestowing initiation (*dīkṣā*) and must have reached at least fifty years of age. However, there may be defects in the teacher’s *kalkasa* (the residual impressions of past actions). Because of these, his appearance may be contrary to what is expected. Such a person is unfit for initiation, even if he has reached an advanced age; for it is not permitted to conceal the defects of the venerable rites of fire-sacrifice (*homa*), initiation, and so forth. This is because if the ascetic (*viku*) does not strive for the excellence of the venerable ritual of initiation, his speech will lack flavor, and his words will be repeatedly flawed and tasteless. He will not know the venerable *Antyādhvā* (the path of the end), and he will be a disgrace to the supreme Lord of Yogins. If such a person performs an initiation, it serves only as a cause for him to receive special honors and praise from the people. Conversely, one who acts contrary to this and receives special honors during the venerable *Paramāntyeṣṭi* (the final funeral rite) will return in the future with contempt; he will incur a great transgression (*mahāpātaka*), for his mind has departed from the course of right conduct (*nyāyapravṛtti*). As for the one who is fit for initiation: he must truly know the venerable teachings of the ritual of initiation. He must possess mastery over the *kalkasa* of the venerable *Antyādhvā*. He must have extensive knowledge of the venerable *Upadeśa* (esoteric instructions). He must be constantly diligent in his practice (*abhyāsa*), powerful in his recitation (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), fire-sacrifice (*homa*), and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). He must not be weary of the service to the Sun (*sūryasevana*) and must never neglect his daily observances. He must know the *yama*, *niyama*, and *vrata*, and he must be affectionate toward his disciples. He must not lack the necessary permissions (*avaravarah*), for if he has many disciples, they will inevitably fall away from the boundaries of proper conduct and logic. As for the scriptural authority (*śruti*) regarding this:"
From pampering arise many faults; from striking arise many virtues.
Therefore, a wise man should administer a beating to his son and his pupil.

[VS_appendix-12j§1] What is it? It is that which consists of nurturing the intellect and satisfying the desires of the mind. One should avoid manifesting faults; however, if there is a reason for striking, one should do so sparingly. One should be sparing with praise. This is why children, sons, and disciples become arrogant. Thus it is said by the wise: "Do not neglect the cultivation of virtues at any time; do not be one who is easily led astray. Indeed, there is no need to be overly concerned about rebuking them.
"O son, this is indeed a sign that the intellect of my son has become turbid. It is as if he were speaking in a delirium; for if it were so, the nature of his illness would have become manifest."
For instance, some children, being untrained, either through their father’s negligence or out of excessive affection,
go astray and, shunned by all people, bring reproach upon their father and great infamy.

[VS_appendix-13j§1] What? The mother’s conduct is not learned; it is shameful. That best of sons is ever wavering due to his father’s negligence. He is constantly preoccupied with the cause of his mother; he chooses the cause of his mother’s affection rather than that of his father. When a son is thus, he has gone astray from the path; he is clearly exposed to the censure of the world and its logic. He is shunned by all people and despised by everyone. Such is the nature of the mother’s bad character; it alone brings disgrace upon the father, being the cause of excessive fault. In short, the mother’s behavior is wicked; it is clearly reflected in her own kind. Thus, she becomes an object of hatred for those who love her.
Nevertheless, some children, having been well-trained by their father’s efforts or out of his great affection,
being virtuous and praised by the multitude of people, truly carry on their father’s great fame through their own qualities.

[VS_appendix-14j§1] If there is no fault in a disciple who has been well-trained according to the instruction of the best of Vinaya masters—whether through the father’s (the teacher’s) effort, the effort of his own parents, or out of great affection, such that the father’s effort for the sake of the child reaches its ultimate fulfillment—then when he is thus, he is clearly seen to possess good character (*suśīlina*). Why? Because of his excellent character (*śīla*), he is praised by the multitude of all people; he is lauded by the entire assembly of men. This is the fame of the father, which is caused by the virtues (of the son). It is exactly so. For this reason, a monk (*viku*) must not fail to exert himself in protecting his sons and disciples, lest he incur sin (*pātaka*). For a son who transgresses the boundaries of propriety (*maryādā-yukti*)—even if he is already grown and has completed his consecrations (*saṃskāra*), reaching the age of adulthood—is certain to fall into the world of hell (*nirayaloka*) at the end of his life. He is abandoned by his father and cast into the depths by the forces of Yama. Such is the fate of a teacher whose disciple behaves improperly; even if the disciple is already mature, the teacher follows him to the world of Yama. Therefore, a monk must not fail to strive in the consecrations performed for them, nor in instructing them in their conduct, their boundaries, and how they should uphold the sacred vows (*brata*). Furthermore, he must observe whether they are capable of attaining the state of a noble being (*kabhujaṅga*) and whether their lineage is worthy of being honored by monks. One must not fail to honor those worthy of consecration. Punishing those who are worthy in such a manner does not cause one to sink into the earth of Java; for this reason, a monk must strive for those who are fit for consecration, so that they may attain the supreme state (*uttamapada*). However, there are those who are unworthy of consecration—grandchildren or distant descendants—who are not permitted to uphold the sacred vows. Even if their conduct is observed to be good, they are nevertheless consecrated merely as a sign of affection. In such a case, it is not improper to punish them. (Suvarṇa 6, Māṣa 4). Likewise, the punishment administered by the elders, disciples, and the Lord Teacher (*bhaṭāra guru*) toward the monk’s disciple is intended to correct him when he is negligent in his instructions. Only those who are fit for consecration are subject to this, because of the gravity of their actions and the severity of their misconduct. If a disciple is like this, one must not hastily forgive him, nor must one repeatedly scold him. One should distinguish between the teacher and the teacher’s son; one should not forgive those who are unfit to be forgiven. One must not act in such a way. Furthermore, if the disciple is not fit to be questioned, one should distinguish the cases. One must not act in such a way. However, if the teacher’s intent is not to stray from the principles of the teaching (*śāsana-yukti*) and is based on the authority of the sacred scriptures (*śāstrāgama*), then one must not be swayed by the impulse of affection when forgiving, nor by anger when questioning. Such a person truly adheres to the state of a noble being. This is solely to purify the wisdom of the monk.

[VS_appendix-14j§2] Now, as for that which is called *vārtā* (news/affair), it is not something to be measured; its nature is as follows: there is one who holds a philosophical tenet (*siddhānta*) concerning the great ones—drinking liquor, a monk (*viku*), killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), being fallen (*patita*), violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpaka*), and theft (*steya*).

[VS_appendix-15j§1] Brahmin-slaughter (*brahmahatyā*) is not like any other human transgression. I have fallen by violating my mother, a sister, a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a wife, a female relative, a woman of high rank, a woman of noble lineage, a woman of the *varaṅ* caste, a woman of the *mantu* caste, a woman of the *rāma* caste, or a woman of the *rabini* caste. Adultery (*gurutalpaka*) means to violate the wife of one’s teacher; furthermore, her descendants are likewise [excluded]. Theft (*steya*) is taking what is not given: stealing from a village, stealing from a caravan, stealing from a house, or even if it be small, stealing from a field, a garden, or a storehouse—it is not permitted to steal any of these. Furthermore, if one violates the wife of a son, the wife of a teacher’s son, or any woman protected by a teacher—even if she is not the actual wife of the teacher, because she is a woman protected by him, the teacher incurs the sin of a mortal transgression (*pātaka*) if he should protect her [from punishment]. Thus it is with the sons of the teacher. It is a mortal transgression for the teacher if he protects them.

Furthermore, there may be a disciple who commits a transgression against his preceptor. Time and again, the preceptor rebukes him for that transgression, yet he does not grant him the status of a *pantên* (one who has undergone purification). Nevertheless, because of his absolute acceptance [of the teachings], he desires to further rectify his moral conduct (*śīla*). This is not permissible for the preceptor if he does not provide assistance; rather, it is when the disciple is weary of his own faults. Time and again, he returns to his preceptor. Such is the nature of this matter; thus is the conduct of a monk toward his disciple. This is according to the sacred tradition (*śruti*). Now, as for the ritual bath (*snāna*):

The *āgneya* bath is with ashes; the *vāruṇa* bath is with a flood of water;
the *brāhmya* bath is indeed by means of mantras; and the *vāyavya* bath is with the dust of cows.

The characteristic of the *āgneya* bath is ash; the characteristic of the *vāruṇa* bath is immersion in water; the characteristic of the *brāhmya* bath is the recitation of mantras; and as for the *vāyavya* bath, its characteristic is to rub the body from the feet up to the head, starting with the soles of the feet and the navel.
The muttering of prayers is the mental bath, while the worship at the three junctions of the day constitutes the ritual service;
touching the earth from a full sacred bathing site is called the earthly bath.

[VS_appendix-18j§1] Bathing, the ritual characteristics, mantra recitation, and twilight worship—these are not merely mental acts. Bathing has various causes, such as visiting a sacred bathing place (*puṇyatīrtha*) on earth; this is one type of earthly [bathing]. Such are the forms of twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*), which serve as indicators for the practitioner (*saṅ viku*).
One who has bathed in knowledge is the highest "bathed" one; so too is one who has bathed through observances and vows. But he is not truly bathed at all if he does not bathe with ashes.

[VS_appendix-19j§1] Abandon that which is called bathing; know that true bathing is through knowledge. Renounce bathing with water, along with its rules and vows. This is the Kali age; it is only that which is known as bathing by the learned that is truly bathing—namely, bathing with ashes. For ashes are the specific excellence of bathing.
Food mixed with worms, insects, and hairs— a wise man, having purified it by scattering ashes over it, may eat even if the minute, invisible impurities remain.

[VS_appendix-20j§1] Whatever food is impure—hair, worms, and so forth; namely: excrement, body hair, nails, mucus, saliva, and insects; such is its nature. Even if it is not recognized as having a cause for impurity and is not visible due to its subtlety, there is no fault for the ascetic (*viku*) who eats that impure food. For it is pure by virtue of being consumed with *bhasma* (sacred ash), accompanied by the exertion of *prāṇāyāma*.
Having burned away defects through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and sin through concentrations (dhāraṇā),
one should withdraw the sense objects by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and the non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna).

Prāṇāyāma suppresses the *doṣas*; *dhāraṇā* suppresses the *kleśas*; *pratyāhāra* suppresses the sense objects (*viṣayas*); and *dhyāna* suppresses the *guṇas* without distinction. This is further the method for the practitioner (*saṅ viku*).
Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger— this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma.

[VS_appendix-22j§1] *Artha* is wealth. *Dhṛti* is firmness of mind. *Kṣamā* is the pacification of anger. *Dama* is the restraint of the intellect. *Asteya* is not being covetous. *Śauca* is that which consists of bathing with ashes and so forth. *Indriyanigraha* is the withdrawal of the senses. *Hrī* is modesty. *Vidyā* is the practice of learning. *Satya* is that which is not false. *Akrodha* is not being prone to anger. All these together are called the tenfold duty (*daśadharma*).
Purity, sacrifice, austerity, charity, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ,
vows, fasting, silence, and bathing— these are the ten observances (niyamas).
Purity (*śauca*) means being constantly clean. Sacrifice (*ijyā*) means worship. Austerity (*tapas*) means the control of the mind and the senses.

Austerity (*tapas*) consists of giving (*dāna*), serving others (*veveh*), reciting the *svādhyāya* (the sacred scriptures), practicing mental sciences such as *balavidyā* and *mahāvidyā*, restraining the genitals (*upastha-nigraha*) by abstaining from sexual intercourse, observing vows (*vrata*) such as fasting (*upavāsa*), maintaining equanimity amidst impurities during meditative absorption (*samādhi*), fasting (*upavāsa*) which is the abstention from food, silence (*mauna*) which is remaining within the mouth, and bathing (*snāna*) which is cleansing the body with water while employing mantras and other rituals. These are the ten that constitute the observances (*niyama*).
Compassion, tranquility, truthfulness, non-violence, self-restraint, straightforwardness,
serenity, sweetness, meditation, and gentleness— these are the ten *yamas*.

[VS_appendix-24j§1] Kindness (*ānṛśaṃsya*) is not praising oneself nor disparaging others; tranquility (*śama*) is the state of being calm; truthfulness (*satya*) is not deceiving; non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is not being mentally agitated; self-restraint (*dama*) is the clarity of one's intellect; meditation (*dhyāna*) is contemplating the true nature of the Lord; serenity (*prasāda*) is benevolence toward others, acting for their welfare; sweetness (*mādhurya*) is the quality of pleasant speech and gentle conduct; gentleness (*mṛdutā*) is being soft in speech—these ten are what constitute *yama*.
Those twice-born who recite the ten stations of Dharma and,
having studied them, live according to them, go to the supreme goal.

[VS_appendix-25j§1] O twice-born, abandon! Abandon the ten-fold states. One who possesses these three qualities truly embodies the ten-fold dharma: the simultaneous pronunciation of the mantra, constant practice, and freedom from sloth during the day and night. Such a one attains the supreme goal and reaches the state of the divine beings. This is the meaning of the venerable *vratiśāsana* as it is understood; therefore, it must not be disregarded by the ascetic (*viku*) who desires purification, nor should he fail to bestow it upon those who have been initiated. Furthermore, he must strive to conform to the injunctions of the *Śruti*, for the purpose of bringing worldly conduct and worldly activity into alignment with that understanding.
Śaradā Rāṇī: This stanza is not in the main text.

[VS_appendix-25(ka)s-ab] Those who have fallen away from the conduct of Śūdras and Mlecchas, as well as the ritual acts of atheists—[VS_appendix-25(ka)s-cd] where could those virtuous ones, who follow the Lord’s partial incarnations, perform such acts while bearing weapons?
(The manuscripts read: *kūryaḥ sāṃśajān anugāḥ?*)

[VS_appendix-25ka_j§1] A verse concerning the meaning: Those who are not fit to be called *agavayakna* (those who have not attained the goal) are the *santa* (the virtuous), the *viku* (ascetics), and all the *para* and *ācārya* (teachers). Then there are those whose actions involve the transition of births (*cyutajanma*) and various types of deaths (*cyutaka*). Furthermore, there are those whose actions involve *śūdras* and *mlecchas*. A *śūdra* is one who engages in buying, selling, and so forth; this is the *madolavli* (the way of the Madola). The *mlecchavṛtti* (the livelihood of the Mleccha) is one who engages in the activities of the *caṇḍāla* caste. *Nāstikriya* (atheistic action) refers to the activities of the *tarəṅ* (the "waves" or lower beings); they are without consciousness. The *tarəṅ* are the lineages of wild animals, beasts, birds, and snakes; they are without consciousness, being the lineages of those possessed by spirits (*mtu saṅe*).

(Em. saṅkeṅ? Kayukayu: "I am one who does not hold weapons; I have no practice nor mastery in the application of the *sañjatas* according to their proper sequence. Furthermore, there is the application of *sañjatas* by the Mlecchas, and the application of *sañjatas* by those who are not [true] warriors—all these are such. How could it not be fitting for a holy man (*santa*) to practice them? It is appropriate for those following the common people. Its form is as follows: *aṃśa savetbetira* (?)."

O people, all of you, listen! This is the essence of every transformation and the nature of the world. Such is the manner of the arising and passing away; it is not fitting to be attached to things in this way. For if one does not exert effort toward this, one will clearly stray from the path of right conduct due to the lack of moral discipline and wisdom.
Thus concludes the Saṅ hyaṅ Vratiśāsana.

[VS_appendix-25ka_j§3] Let there be no granting of that consecration (*saṃskāra*) by a priest who lacks the mental disposition (*manaḥ-saṃskāra*), even if he is worthy of receiving the initiation (*dīkṣita*) from His Majesty. If the disciple does not possess the inner realization (*ātman*) regarding the ultimate goal of the venerable teaching of the observances (*vratiśāsana*), his consecration is deficient. If there is a priest who performs such a consecration, his punishment shall be three *suvarṇas* and two months [of service]. Furthermore, if he possesses great knowledge of the venerable teaching of the observances but does not cause his disciples to realize it through their own consecration, his punishment shall be one *suvarṇa* and three months [of service]. Regarding the realization of his fellow teachers concerning the ultimate goal of the venerable teaching of the observances, they must strive for it constantly and with focused attention. 0.
Oṃ, homage be to the Lord of the Gaṇas! Oṃ, homage to Brahmā! Oṃ, homage to Sarasvatī! May there be well-being; may there be long life! 0 ||
